title: Seven-day sighting delays permit zero butterfly-minus-swallow warmth slopes in Japan under one-day annual change limits, 1953-2020
abstract: We tested how detection delays affect a published link between spring temperature and relative butterfly and swallow first sightings. We used the same 4,077 paired station-years at 69 Japan stations in 1953-2020 and rebuilt the panel from raw public data. Four region and period models had recorded slopes of -1.70 to -2.22 days per C. If each species delay is zero to seven days and can change by at most one day per elapsed year, sharp conditional slope bounds include both signs in all four samples. The minimum annual limits for zero are 0.71-0.89 day per species. If only one species delay can vary under the same limits, all four fitted slopes remain negative. We give exact bounds, delay sequences, independent solver checks and an offline reproduction. The delays are assumptions, not measured errors. These bounds do not include sampling uncertainty or correct missing observations. Selected records, unknown effort and abundance, coarse weather and weather windows that extend past sightings limit biological interpretation. The result does not identify actual onset, a causal climate effect, pollution effects or a harmful timing mismatch.

display.caption: Fitted slopes and sharp delay bounds in four Japan samples. Green permits variable delays in both species; brown permits a variable delay in one species. Each delay is zero to seven days and changes by at most one day per elapsed year. These are conditional bounds, not confidence intervals.
Allowed slopes as the annual delay change limit increases. Each species delay is at most seven days. No distribution of actual delay is estimated.

citations.reason: Reuse the verified paired sighting panel and source build code. Test the sensitivity of the same four reported slopes to unmeasured detection delay.
Prior method for paired-date sensitivity with capped delays and annual change limits. We transfer this method to two animal first-detection series and compare one and two variable delays.
Prior evidence of animal and plant timing differences and mixed evidence for detection bias in the same JMA archive.
